unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Facilities for Exporters and Importers

facts.statement: The Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS), operational from 1 March 2014, lets authorised dealer banks report on a single platform and integrates returns on shipping bills of caution-listed exporters, delayed utilisation of advances received for exports, and exports outstanding beyond the stipulated period. Banks record advance remittances received for exports, extensions of time for realisation and write-offs in it, and no longer file a separate return for export bills outstanding beyond the stipulated period. Banks keep an Export Bills Register aligned with EDPMS, with bill numbers on a financial year basis.
facts.locator: Printed p. 149, section 5.6; RBI Export Master Direction C.14, C.15 and C.23

facts.statement: Banks must watch export bills closely; where a bill stays outstanding beyond the due date, the bank takes it up with the exporter, and if the exporter neither delivers the proceeds nor seeks extension in time, the bank reports to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank. Duplicate EDF or SOFTEX forms stay with the bank until the full proceeds are realised, except for undrawn balances. Laxity in follow-up is viewed seriously and may invoke the penal provisions of FEMA. The Reserve Bank caution-lists an exporter on the recommendation of the authorised dealer where the exporter has come to the adverse notice of the Enforcement Directorate, CBI, DRI or another agency, is not traceable, or is not making sincere efforts to realise proceeds; the bank also recommends de-caution-listing.
facts.locator: Export Master Direction C.15 and C.28; S03 printed p. 149

facts.statement: Authorised dealer banks may factor export receivables on a non-recourse basis on conditions including: a bank decides on its own whether to enter into such an arrangement; it ensures the client is not over-financed; the invoices represent genuine trade invoices; the export factor has an arrangement with an import factor for credit evaluation and collection; a notation on the invoice says the importer must pay the import factor; after factoring the export factor may close the export bills and report in EDPMS; where there is a single factor with no import factor overseas, credit evaluation details may be obtained from the correspondent bank abroad; and KYC and due diligence on the exporter are ensured. Exim Bank and authorised dealer banks may undertake forfaiting of export receivables.
facts.locator: Export Master Direction A.12 and A.13

facts.statement: Factoring is a continuing arrangement under which a factor purchases an exporter's book debts on open account sales, with or without recourse, and controls credit and administers the sales ledger. A factor provides debt administration (managing the sales ledger and collection), credit protection (credit intelligence and assessment of buyers) and factor financing, normally advancing up to 75% to 80% of outstanding debts. In an international factoring deal the client sends invoices to the export factor, which gives finance up to the approved extent and passes an invoice copy to the import factor in the importer's country; the import factor collects on the due date and remits to the export factor; if the debtor does not pay, the import factor steps into the shoes of the export factor for recovery. Systems include single factor, two factor, direct export factoring and direct import factoring. Advantages: immediate finance up to 75-80%, no letter of credit needed, credit checks, sales ledger maintenance, credit protection and advice on new markets.

Forfaiting is the discounting of export receivables, without recourse to the exporter, for a medium term at a fixed rate, for the full value of the contract or invoice. It is a source of finance and not credit insurance, and the financier takes the importer's standing, country risk and often the guarantee of the importer's bank into account. It is done against a bill of exchange or promissory note accepted by the importer and guaranteed by its bank (avalised). Charges comprise a commitment fee (the courseware says usually between 0.50 and 1.50 per cent a year on the unutilised portion, non-refundable), discount charges based on market rates for the credit period plus a margin for the forfaiter's risk, and documentation fees. Benefits: removes political and commercial risk, 100% finance, no recourse, freedom from credit administration, saving on credit insurance and a fixed rate.

The courseware compares factoring and forfaiting: factoring suits on-going open account sales not backed by letters of credit or accepted bills; it is short term, can be with or without recourse, needs a continuous arrangement routing all sales through the factor, the factor assumes responsibility for collection, charges cover financing, collection, administration, credit protection and information, and it is common for domestic and international transactions. Forfaiting suits one-off transactions backed by letters of credit or accepted (avalised) bills; it is medium to long term (one to five years), generally without recourse, deals are transaction-wise with no need to route other business, the forfaiter's responsibility covers the forfaited debt only, charges include discount and commitment charges, and it is for international transactions only.

payload.title: EDPMS: one screen for every export bill
payload.core_explanation_md:
The **Export Data Processing and Monitoring System (EDPMS)** has run since **1 March 2014**. It gives authorised dealer banks **one platform** to report and monitor exports.

It **brings together** what used to be separate returns on:
- shipping bills of **caution-listed** exporters;
- **delayed use** of advances received for exports;
- exports **outstanding beyond the stipulated period**.

Banks record in it: **advance remittances** for exports, **extensions of time** for realisation, and **write-offs**. They no longer send a separate return for bills outstanding too long: the data is visible in EDPMS.

Banks also keep an **Export Bills Register**, in line with EDPMS, **numbering bills April to March**.

payload.title: Chasing overdue export bills, and the caution list
payload.core_explanation_md:
**The bank's duty**: watch every bill. If it is **overdue**, take it up with the exporter. If the exporter does not **deliver the proceeds or ask for an extension** in time, **report to the Reserve Bank's Regional Office**, with the reason if known.

**Documents**: the **duplicate EDF or SOFTEX** stays with the bank until **full realisation** (except for undrawn balances).

**Consequence of laxity**: seen **seriously** by RBI; **FEMA penal provisions** may be invoked.

**Caution list**: the RBI lists an exporter **on the bank's recommendation** where the exporter has come to the adverse notice of the **ED, CBI, DRI** or another agency, is **not traceable**, or is **not making sincere efforts** to realise proceeds. The bank also recommends **de-listing**. A caution-listed exporter is told of the listing and the outstanding shipping bills, and bills are accepted only on conditions.

payload.title: Factoring: a service that buys the invoices and runs the ledger
payload.core_explanation_md:
**What**: an ongoing arrangement where a **factor buys an exporter's book debts** from **open account** sales, **with or without recourse**, and manages credit control and the **sales ledger**.

**Three services**
1. **Debt administration**: keeps the ledger, chases payment.
2. **Credit protection**: assesses buyers' credit.
3. **Factor financing**: advances **75% to 80%** of the outstanding invoices.

**International chain**: exporter → **export factor** (finances) → **import factor** in the buyer's country (collects on the due date and remits). If the debtor does **not pay**, the import factor **steps into the export factor's shoes** to recover.

**Systems**: **single factor**; **two factor**; **direct export** factoring; **direct import** factoring.

**Why exporters use it**: immediate finance, **no letter of credit**, credit checks, ledger work done, credit protection and advice on new markets.

payload.title: What banks must check before factoring export receivables without recourse
Forfaiting: selling a medium-term receivable for cash, with no come-back
payload.core_explanation_md:
**What**: the financier **discounts** medium-term export receivables **without recourse** to the exporter, at a **fixed rate**, for the **full value**.

**Not insurance**: it is **finance**. The forfaiter judges the **importer's standing**, the **country risk**, and often relies on the **guarantee of the importer's bank**.

**The paper**: a **bill of exchange or promissory note** accepted by the importer and **guaranteed (avalised) by its bank**.

**What it costs**
- **Commitment fee**: usually **0.50% to 1.50% a year** on the unutilised part, **non-refundable**.
- **Discount charge**: a **market-related** rate for the period **plus a margin** for risk.
- **Documentation fees**.

**Benefits to the exporter**: **political and commercial risk** removed, **100% finance**, **no recourse**, no collection work, no credit insurance cost, **fixed rate**.

payload.title: Factoring or forfaiting? A side-by-side
payload.core_explanation_md:
| | **Factoring** | **Forfaiting** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Backed by** | On-going **open account** sales, no LC | **One-off** deals backed by an **LC** or **avalised bill** |
| **Term** | **Short** | **Medium to long** (1 to 5 years) |
| **Recourse** | **With or without** | Generally **without** |
| **Arrangement** | **Continuous**; all sales routed through the factor | **Transaction-wise** |
| **Collection** | Factor **assumes** collection | Only for the **forfaited debt** |
| **Charges** | Financing, collection, administration, credit protection | **Discount and commitment** |
| **Scope** | **Domestic and international** | **International only** |

payload.title: Two financing calculations: a factored invoice and a forfaited bill
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case A (factoring): an exporter factors invoices of USD 250,000; the factor advances 80% at once and charges 1.2% of the invoice value for its services (ignore interest on the advance). What is the advance, and what balance is paid on the due date? Illustrative case B (forfaiting): a forfaiter buys an avalised bill of USD 500,000 due in 180 days at a discount rate of 6% a year (360-day year) and charges a commitment fee of 1% a year on the contract value for 90 days. What does the exporter receive?

worked_steps.description: A: service charges at 1.2% of the invoice value.
A: balance on the due date, after the advance and charges.
B: discount for 180 days at 6% on a 360-day year.
B: commitment fee, 1% a year for 90 days.
B: net proceeds to the exporter.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: Factoring: advance USD 200,000.00 and a balance of USD 47,000.00 on the due date. Forfaiting: the exporter receives USD 483,750.00 and carries no recourse

self_check.prompt_text: Which of the two leaves the exporter exposed to a buyer's default?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Factoring with recourse can; forfaiting is without recourse, so the exporter is not exposed.

payload.stem_md: A forfaiter buys an avalised bill of USD 800,000 due in 120 days at a discount rate of 5.4% a year on a 360-day year. What discount does it deduct, in USD?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the answer to 2 decimal places.

worked_solution_steps.description: Discount for 120 days at 5.4% a year

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is recorded in EDPMS, according to RBI's directions and the courseware?

options.text_md: Only the import bills of the bank
options.explanation_md: EDPMS covers exports.

options.text_md: Only the letters of credit issued by the bank
options.explanation_md: EDPMS monitors export data.

options.text_md: Advance remittances received for exports, extensions of time for realisation, and write-offs of export bills
options.explanation_md: These are all recorded in EDPMS.

options.text_md: Only bills of lading
options.explanation_md: EDPMS records export transactions and their realisation, not bills of lading as such.

payload.correct_explanation_md: EDPMS records advance remittances for exports, extensions of time for realisation and write-offs, among other export data.

payload.stem_md: An exporter has not delivered proceeds of an overdue bill and has not asked for an extension. What must the authorised dealer do?

options.text_md: Write the bill off at once
options.explanation_md: Write-off is subject to conditions and limits.

options.text_md: Return the duplicate EDF to the exporter
options.explanation_md: Duplicate EDF stays with the bank until realisation.

options.text_md: Take no action until the exporter responds
options.explanation_md: Banks must follow up systematically and vigorously.

options.text_md: Report the matter to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank, with the reason if known
options.explanation_md: This is the required step.

payload.correct_explanation_md: If the exporter fails to deliver the proceeds or seek an extension in time, the bank reports to the Regional Office of the Reserve Bank, stating where possible the reason for the delay.

payload.stem_md: On whose recommendation does the Reserve Bank place an exporter on its caution list?

options.text_md: The exporter itself
options.explanation_md: An exporter does not recommend its own listing.

options.text_md: The authorised dealer bank concerned
options.explanation_md: The bank recommends listing and de-listing to the Regional Office.

options.text_md: The overseas buyer
options.explanation_md: The buyer plays no role in the listing.

options.text_md: The Export Credit Guarantee Corporation
options.explanation_md: ECGC keeps a separate list of its own.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank caution-lists an exporter on the recommendation of the authorised dealer bank concerned.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is a condition for an authorised dealer factoring export receivables without recourse?

options.text_md: The bank ensures the client is not over-financed and that the invoices represent genuine trade invoices
options.explanation_md: Both are conditions.

options.text_md: The bank may factor any invoice, genuine or not, if it is insured
options.explanation_md: Genuine trade invoices are required.

options.text_md: No arrangement with an import factor is ever needed
options.explanation_md: An arrangement with an import factor, or correspondent credit details for a single factor, is needed.

options.text_md: The exporter must give a letter of credit
options.explanation_md: Factoring is for open account sales without an LC.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The bank must ensure the client is not over-financed and that the invoices are genuine trade invoices, among other conditions.

payload.stem_md: What share of outstanding invoices does a factor typically advance to the client, according to the courseware?

options.explanation_md: 100% finance is a feature of forfaiting.
This understates the advance.
This is the typical advance.

options.text_md: 50% fixed
options.explanation_md: No such fixed share is stated.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A factor is normally willing to advance up to 75% to 80% of the outstanding debts.

payload.stem_md: What is the legal position of the exporter in a forfaiting transaction?

options.text_md: With recourse: the exporter repays if the importer defaults
options.explanation_md: That describes factoring with recourse.

options.text_md: The exporter is the guarantor of the avalised bill
options.explanation_md: The importer's bank is the guarantor.

options.text_md: The exporter must buy credit insurance
options.explanation_md: Forfaiting saves the cost of credit insurance.

options.text_md: Without recourse: the forfaiter bears the risk of non-payment
options.explanation_md: Forfaiting is generally without recourse.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Forfaiting is without recourse to the exporter, so political and commercial risks pass to the forfaiter.

payload.stem_md: Which pairing of transaction type and product is correct?

options.text_md: On-going open account sales: forfaiting; one-off deal backed by an avalised bill: factoring
options.explanation_md: The products are the other way round.

options.text_md: On-going open account sales: factoring; one-off medium-term export backed by an avalised bill: forfaiting
options.explanation_md: This pairing matches the comparison.

options.text_md: Short-term domestic sales: forfaiting
options.explanation_md: Forfaiting is for international transactions.

options.text_md: One-year to five-year export bills: factoring
options.explanation_md: That is the forfaiting term.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Factoring suits continuing open account sales; forfaiting suits one-off, medium-term transactions backed by an LC or an avalised bill.

payload.stem_md: Which of the following is a typical element of the cost of forfaiting?

options.text_md: A commitment fee on the unutilised portion of the contract value, which is non-refundable
options.explanation_md: The commitment fee is a typical element.

options.text_md: A refundable deposit of 10% of the bill
options.explanation_md: No such deposit is stated.

options.text_md: A credit insurance premium
options.explanation_md: Forfaiting saves the cost of credit insurance.

options.text_md: A fee for maintaining the sales ledger
options.explanation_md: That is a factoring service.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Forfaiting charges include a non-refundable commitment fee on the unutilised portion, discount charges and documentation fees.

payload.stem_md: From which date has EDPMS been operational, according to the courseware?

options.text_md: 1 April 2016
options.explanation_md: This is the date of the MCLR linkage.

options.text_md: 1 January 2016
options.explanation_md: This is the date of RBI's Master Directions.

options.text_md: 1 March 2014
options.explanation_md: EDPMS was operationalised on 1 March 2014.

options.text_md: 1 July 2007
options.explanation_md: This is the date of UCP 600.

payload.correct_explanation_md: EDPMS has been operational since 1 March 2014; realisation of export transactions with shipping documents after 28 February 2014 is reported in it.

unresolved: The factoring and forfaiting descriptions, the 75-80% advance and the commitment fee range (0.50% to 1.50% a year) are the courseware's, not RBI rules; the Export Master Direction states only the permissions and conditions in A.12 and A.13. Discount rates in the courseware are LIBOR-based; the items use plain illustrative rates.
RBI's Export Master Direction page used was updated on 17 July 2026, after the cut-off; the sections used (A.12, A.13, C.14, C.15, C.28) were not the ones changed on that date.
The courseware's phrase that Gold Card exporters must not be 'blacklisted by ECGC' differs from the Directions (Specific Approval List); the Directions were taught in the previous batch.
Reviewer for this batch is the authoring agent; no independent or human review.
